newsitem.title: USA: Albright plans trip to Middle East by end-August.
newsitem.headline: Albright plans trip to Middle East by end-August.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday she planned to go to the Middle East at the end of August and would try to speed up work on the "final status" talks for Israeli-Palestinian peace.

Albright, speaking one week after a deadly bombing in Jerusalem, said her trip depended on improvement in the security situation. That would be discussed during a trip by U.S. mediator Dennis Ross starting at the end of this week.
"Provided there is some progress on security issues I am prepared to travel to the Middle East at the end of this month," Albright said in a speech to the National Press Club.

"I will consult closely with the leaders of the region and especially with Israeli and Palestinian leaders to improve the climate for negotiations and to discuss the procedural and substantive aspects of the permanent status issues," she said.
She said there must be an "unrelenting struggle" against extremism. "The Palestinian commitment to fight terror must be constant and absolute. This is essential to move the peace process forward."

She added: "The terrorists are unrelenting and so we must be unrelenting in our struggle against them. on this issue, there can be no winks, no double standards, no double meanings and with respect to the imprisonment of terrorists, no revolving doors."

Albright stressed that the United States would not become a party to the talks but would be there at the table to nudge the parties along. "Only the parties can make the decisions but we will support them," she said.

She said: "If the parties have a clear mutual and favourable sense of the ultimate direction of negotiation, it will be easier for them to overcome setbacks and avoid distractions along the way. This will require accelerating permanent status negotiations. Today this step is urgent and important," she said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already proposed rapid "final status" negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians to wind up in six months, instead of the original 1999 deadline.
Those talks are meant to settle the borders and nature of the Palestinian entity -- Palestinians themselves want an independent state -- and the administration of Jerusalem.

Albright has been in contact with the leaders in the region by telephone and during their visits to Washington but has resisted travelling to the Middle East herself until she felt sure concrete progress could be made.

The Clinton administration has come under pressure to intervene actively as talks between Israelis and Palestinians became mired over Israel's decision to erect housing settlements in traditionally Arab areas.

But Albright stressed this could not justify a violent Palestinian response. "There is no moral equivalency between suicide bombers and bulldozers but the principle of refraining from unhelpful unilateral acts is essential to maintaining mutual confidence," she said.

"We now face a crisis of confidence that has put at risk past gains and rekindled old animosities," Albright said, adding that restoration of a sense of security was essential if the peace process was to be rebuilt. "This is basic. This is common sense," she said.

"The popular desire for peace is durable, resilient and strong. This is what extremists and terrorists fear the most and this is why, despite the bombing this past week and despite threats of further violence, the process of peacemaking has survived and will continue to survive," she said.

Reasserting U.S. policy, she said: "We seek a just and lasting peace achieved through direct negotiations, based on UN Security Council resolutions 242 and 338, including the principle on which every Arab-Israeli agreement has been built: land for peace."
Netanyahu has rejected the original basis of the Middle East peace talks: Israel trading occupied Arab land for peace with its Arab neighbours.
